speakers: Andrew Beer (co-host, DBMF managed-futures replication ETF)
summary: Dec 2025 Systematic Investor: Beer and Kaastrup-Larsen discuss the shift away from 60/40 as bonds stopped diversifying, why a 10-market replication ETF (DBMF) beat the CTA index in 2025, a Simplify index-based CTA ETF and the true-cost debate for swaps vs fees, and how to explain trend following ('cloudy crystal ball', someone knows something). Also Nordic roundtable on short-term vs long-term models and alpha/beta separation.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the the playbook of 6040 just stopped working
claims.claim: In this decade bonds stopped working as a diversifier, behaving like lousy equity exposure (lower returns, similar drawdown, higher volatility), pushing allocators to add a diversifying 'other' bucket.
claims.direction: less bonds, more diversifiers such as managed futures

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: manager futures is one of those really statistically obvious allocations. If you give them uh easy and efficient ways of investing to it,
claims.claim: Managed futures is a statistically obvious diversifier but is still zero in many portfolios; easy ETF access could make it standard.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they were actually expecting more money going into liquid alternatives, not so much these illlquid alternatives
claims.claim: Goldman expects wealth allocations flowing more to liquid alternatives than illiquid ones; large managers (BlackRock, Fidelity, Invesco) are launching trend ETFs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they asked him about the multistrat, the pot shops and what his prediction was for them. And actually he was not particularly bullish about their uh ability um going forward.
claims.claim: Dalio is not bullish on multi-manager pod shops because internal competition makes them uncollegial; pod shops are the current hot alternative.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I can't believe that your 300th team is as good as your fifth team that you've hired.
claims.claim: Pod shops face diminishing team quality as inflows grow, yet they have defied naysayers for years with leverage and risk controls.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: one of the things in our portfolios is obviously we're more concentrated in our positions and usually uh sometimes there's idiosyncratic risk associated with that.
claims.claim: A 10-market replication portfolio is more concentrated than diversified CTAs, so it carries idiosyncratic risk (more short yen helped; more short euro hurt in 2025).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: just how contrarian it was to maintain this kind of bullish position in the let it run hot trade um after liberation day.
claims.claim: Trend followers that stayed long equities after Liberation Day were contrarian and early; many human strategists capitulated.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: complexity actually hurt portfolios. The more positions you had in more esoteric markets if you're getting whipsaw you were getting whipsaw more there.
claims.claim: After Liberation Day secondary and esoteric markets were more volatile than major ones, so portfolios with many exotic markets were whipsawed more.
claims.testable: yes - compare core vs wide universe

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we're always looking back in a you know pretty short rear it's a rearview window but it's a pretty short rearview window. um uh you know we can be a little bit slower to derisk and that definitely helped us
claims.claim: A replication fund with a short but not very short lookback was slower to de-risk, which helped when the shock reversed (about 500bp of 2025 outperformance came in days after Liberation Day).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe instead of it being a replication strategy to me maybe it's kind of an alternative data strategy
claims.claim: Replication using fund exposures yields tracking error, so it is closer to an alternative-data CTA than a true tracker.
claims.indicator: tracking error vs SG CTA index

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we really tried to aim for for stock gench and index plus 400 basis points.
claims.claim: The replication design assumed hedge-fund index costs (management, incentive, implementation) of about 200bp conservatively, targeting index plus 400bp, and it delivered that or more.
claims.indicator: SG CTA index; replication of 10 factors

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: If you can get that same statistical characteristics only 10 instruments then is the signal itself of the space really a major market signal
claims.claim: If 10 major markets reproduce CTA beta, crisis alpha and zero stock-bond correlation, the CTA signal is a major-market signal and extras (shorter-term models, vol controls, exotic markets) may detract.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I actually think it's I I I would actually argue it's almost more of a technological innovation of finding a way to capture that signal
claims.claim: Replication is an efficiency innovation to capture the trend signal, not a diluted version of CTA alpha; the industry largely disagrees.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Btop 50 is down 18 basis point uh 0.18. It's up 1.05%. 05% so far this year.
claims.claim: As of late Nov 2025: BTOP50 +1.05% YTD, SG CTA -3.06%, SG Trend -0.79%, SG Short-Term Traders -5.76% YTD.
claims.indicator: BTOP50; SG CTA; SG Trend; SG Short-Term Traders

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: our core replication strategy, which is in an ETF in the US and in a use fund in Europe, um, was launched in the middle of 2016 as an active strategy.
claims.claim: The same 10-factor replication has run weekly (Mondays) since July 2016 without change, now with a 9.5-year track record in different vehicles.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you can't actually, it's not like if you benchmark a manager to the S&P 500, you have a default.
claims.claim: Wealth managers lack a tradable index for CTA exposure, so an index around the replication strategy lets allocators model and benchmark it with long history (and via swaps).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: In the US in 2019, there was a change in rules around the use of derivatives and ETFs
claims.claim: The 2019 SEC derivatives rule made derivative-based ETFs easier, enabling trend and managed futures ETFs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they've priced it very low, a 20 basis point management fee and then a 15 basis points of of of acquired fund expenses.
claims.claim: Simplify's index-based managed futures ETF charges 20bp plus 15bp acquired fund expenses; swap costs of accessing the index are not shown in the headline fee.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: 350 basis points of annual outperformance over a decade. Uh the reason it's so pronounced is because there are efficiencies that we've tapped into
claims.claim: Trading 10 liquid futures contracts less often cuts implementation costs, giving about 350bp annual outperformance over a decade versus funds trading hundreds of contracts.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: your $100 might turn over 20 times during the course of a year. 20 times like that may turn over on a on a notional basis, right?
claims.claim: CTAs with short-term models, vol controls and many instruments can turn over notional about 20 times a year, so implementation cost per added instrument (70 to 190 markets) matters.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we do about 350 basis points better than them over time okay three reasons
claims.claim: Versus multi-manager Abby Capital, about 350bp better over time: roughly 100bp from performance differential in the ETF, extra volatility, and 150bp not explained by management fees.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: 80% of the assets have expense ratios still below 20 basis points.
claims.claim: About 80% of US ETF assets cost below 20bp; ETF model portfolios hold only stocks and bonds, with zero diversifier exposure.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: net of fees the sock gen CTNX has done 300 basis points over cash, right? So, so let's say prefee that's 500 basis points
claims.claim: SG Trend index returned about 300bp over cash net of fees, about 500bp before fees, framing fee debates.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it costs 300 basis points to implement this CTA
claims.claim: Implementation costs of a CTA strategy (~300bp) are real costs even if not paid to the manager, and should be compared apples to apples.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: You've got people who report zero transaction costs because the US rules are so bad around calculating transaction costs.
claims.claim: US fund reporting rules allow zero reported transaction costs in some CTA mutual funds, hiding true implementation costs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what I love about the space is that every now and then it's contrarian early and right in a big way
claims.claim: Trend following has episodes where it is contrarian, early and right (short Treasuries Sept 2020, short yen at breakout from 105-110 band, long gold below $3,000).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: someone knows something what do they know that I don't know
claims.claim: Price trending from 10 to 12 signals that someone knows something; trend following latches onto new information (inflation, policy), not sentiment changes, as with the yen from 110 to 160.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they've built these global detectors around these local markets to to get an early warning sign that that something big is changing.
claims.claim: CTAs act as detectors across many markets, signalling major changes early (yen, Treasuries, crude oil in 2022).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if the crystal ball is right we will pick that up. That is our signal. So we don't need the crystal ball actually.
claims.claim: If a forecast is right, the price path will produce the trend signal anyway; trend following captures correct views without needing to forecast.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: You don't need to know what they know. You just need to know that they're buying or selling their own stock.
claims.claim: Prices reveal informed participants voting with their portfolios (like insider buys and sells), so one can follow without knowing what they know.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: It's every 6040 portfolio that was dialing up their exposure to bonds going into 2022 because they needed to rebalance it up.
claims.claim: Trend alpha comes from slow institutional models, such as 60/40 portfolios rebalancing into falling bonds in 2022, which cannot change as the world changes.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: shorterm versus longerterm models. Um uh more more esoteric markets versus versus the core markets.
claims.claim: At the Stockholm roundtable CTAs debated short-term vs long-term models, esoteric vs core markets, risk controls, and AI/alternative data (AQR); equally smart people disagreed on the same data.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's presented with a certainty. you know, we are adding short-term models because by the time it's it's presented
claims.claim: Enhancements such as added short-term models are presented with false certainty, backed by selective evidence, while the business is ultimately human judgement.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you can take more single manager risk if you feel you have the beta solved.
claims.claim: Alpha/beta separation: hold a cheap core replication/beta allocation and then take more single-manager or commodity risk (e.g. AQR, which had a train wreck in prior six years then a strong 5).
